subject: Culture
title: Egyptian Mummification
description: A short lesson to help you apply Egyptian Mummification.

hook.text: The Egyptian embalming process took 70 days. The brain was pulled out through the nose with a hooked tool.

buildup.text: Egyptians believed the body was needed in the afterlife. Preservation was a passport to eternity.

discovery.text: Only elites got full mummification. Commoners were buried in desert sand—which often preserved them just as well.

twist.text: In the 1800s, Europeans ground up mummies for paint pigment called 'mummy brown' and for medicinal powders.

climax.text: CT scans now reveal diseases, diets, and injuries in mummies—3,000-year-old medical records preserved in linen.

punchline.text: They preserved their dead. Their dead preserved their history.

quiz.question: How long did Egyptian mummification take?

details.summary: Egyptian mummification was a 70-day process that preserved the body for eternal life. Priests removed organs, dried the body in natron salt, wrapped it in linen, and placed amulets at specific points. This extraordinary practice reflected the belief that the soul needed its body forever.
details.whyItMatters: Mummification reveals the lengths ancient Egyptians went to defeat death. Their preservation technology influenced medicine, chemistry, and humanity's relationship with mortality for millennia.
takeaways: The full mummification process took approximately 70 days
Organs were removed and stored in canopic jars
Only the brain was discarded — Egyptians considered it useless

faq.question: Why did Egyptians mummify their dead?
faq.answer: Egyptians believed the soul (ka and ba) needed a preserved body to inhabit in the afterlife. If the body decayed, the soul would be lost forever. Mummification ensured the deceased could eat, drink, and live eternally in the Field of Reeds.

faq.question: Why was the brain removed through the nose?
faq.answer: Egyptians considered the heart, not the brain, to be the seat of intelligence and emotion. The brain was extracted through the nostrils using a hooked instrument and discarded. The heart was left in place because it would be weighed against the feather of Ma'at in the afterlife judgment.
